{{Short description|Type of plane curve}}
[[Image:Epispiral.svg|thumb|226px|An epispiral with equation r(&theta;)=2sec(2&theta;)]]
The epispiral is a [[plane curve]] with [[polar equation]] 
:<math>\ r=a \sec{n\theta}</math>.
There are ''n'' sections if ''n'' is odd and 2''n'' if ''n'' is even.

It is the polar or circle [[inversive geometry|inversion]] of the [[rose (mathematics)|rose]] curve.

In [[astronomy]] the epispiral is [[Newton%27s_theorem_of_revolving_orbits#Illustrative_example:_Cotes's_spirals|related to the equations]] that explain [[planet|planets']] orbits.

== Alternative definition ==
There is another definition of the epispiral that has to do with tangents to circles:<ref>{{Cite web |title=construction of the epispiral by tangent lines |url=https://www.desmos.com/calculator/izryfh49p7 |access-date=2023-12-02 |website=Desmos |language=en}}</ref>

Begin with a circle.

Rotate some single point on the circle around the circle by some angle <math>\theta</math> and at the same time by an angle in constant proportion to <math>\theta</math>, say <math>c\theta</math> for some constant <math>c</math>.

The intersections of the tangent lines to the circle at these new points rotated from that single point for every <math>\theta</math> would trace out an epispiral.

The polar equation can be derived through simple geometry as follows:

To determine the polar coordinates <math>(\rho,\phi)</math> of the intersection of the tangent lines in question for some <math>\theta</math> and <math>-1<c<1</math>, note that <math>\phi</math> is halfway between <math>\theta</math> and <math>c\theta</math> by congruence of triangles, so it is <math>\frac{(c+1)\theta}{2}</math>. Moreover, if the radius of the circle generating the curve is <math>r</math>, then since there is a right-angled triangle (it's right-angled as a tangent to a circle meets the radius at a right angle at the point of tangency) with hypotenuse <math>\rho</math> and an angle <math>\frac{(1-c) \theta}{2}</math> to which the adjacent leg of the triangle is <math>r</math>, the radius <math>\rho</math> at the intersection point of the relevant tangents is <math>r\sec(\frac{(1-c)\theta}{2})</math>. This gives the polar equation of the curve, <math>\rho=r\sec(\frac{(1-c)\phi}{c+1})</math> for all points <math>(\rho,\phi)</math> on it.
